    NUS EDIC Final Year Project · AY2026/27

    AI Synthetic Generation of Defect Images

    Synthetic defect image generation for AI-based manufacturing inspection when real defect images are scarce. LoRA models are trained with Kohya_ss and generate new defect images from real photos (image-to-image). An agentic loop, judged by a YOLO classifier trained on real TE images, tunes the hyperparameters so non-specialist users can produce reliable defect images.

    02

    Overview

    Problem statement

    The problem

    New defect classes. Not enough images to learn them.

    When a new connector line goes live, the AI inspection model has to catch defects that have barely happened yet. With only a handful of examples, it can't learn them reliably, and every defect it misses is wasted product. TE Connectivity faces this today: new defect classes have been added to its inspection model's scope, with very few real images to train on.

    10–30real images per defect class
    ~100images per class needed for reliable training
    99%+of production images are defect-free (OK)

    More OK images are easy to collect. More defect images are not, and waiting for them to occur on the line delays the launch.

    Figure . Today's dataset: real images per class, and the synthetic images needed to reach ~100 per defect class. The dashed line marks 100. Hover a bar for numbers.

    Our solution

    Our solution

    From a few defect images to a training-ready dataset.

    Our application learns from a small set of real defect images and generates realistic synthetic ones, then checks and tunes its own output. TE engineers get a balanced, validated dataset in about a week, in time to verify their inspection model before the new line goes live.

    ~25real images per defect class
    Our applicationGenerate · Evaluate · Re-tune
    >100validated images per class
    Without a tuning agent
    • Engineers must understand the generation model and how each parameter changes the images.
    • Wrong settings produce wrong images: two images meant to be NG-Misalign, one came out aligned.
    • Every retry means retraining and regenerating.
    With our application
    • The app evaluates its own images and tunes the settings automatically.
    • Only images that pass the evaluator are kept.
    • Engineers receive a validated dataset, with no generative-AI expertise needed.
    Easy to useA guided application, not scripts
    EfficientFewer wasted retrain cycles
    No GenAI expertiseBuilt for inspection engineers

    Objectives

    1 · Model optimisation

    Improve on the UROP SDXL-LoRA model; now using Realistic Vision 5.1 with text-to-image and image-to-image generation.

    2 · Agent-assisted tuning

    Generated images are evaluated first; settings are tuned only if the images are not good enough, so users don't have to tune hyperparameters by hand.

    2a · Evaluator agent
    • A YOLO26n classifier, trained only on real TE images, checks every generated image.
    • An image passes if its predicted class matches its intended class.
    • The share of images that pass (pass rate) scores each run.
    See Section 7.2 →
    2b · Decision agent
    • Accept (pass rate ≥ 80%): keep the passing images and save the settings. No tuning needed. (80% is set lower for now while data is limited.)
    • Borderline (50–80%): ask the Recommender for settings close to this run.
    • Reject (< 50%): ask the Recommender for different settings.
    2c · Recommender agent

    The Recommender Agent uses Optuna's Tree-structured Parzen Estimator (TPE) to propose LoRA training hyperparameters, reducing the need for manual trial-and-error.

    It currently optimises three parameters: learning rate, LoRA rank and training epochs. Proposed configurations are validated using Pydantic before being passed to subsequent pipeline components.

    Preliminary testing includes simulated optimisation, historical evaluation feedback and integration with the YOLO Evaluation Agent. Full training-based optimisation is planned for Semester 2.

    3 · Reporting

    Per-run experiment report with a keep/reject recommendation, integrated into the AITK web app.

    03

    Background & Prior Work

    A previous UROP team (CDE4301, AY2025/26 Sem 1) compared several generative approaches on TE Connectivity solder-pin welding images and built the AITK toolkit, a guided web app for training and generation. This project starts from their conclusions.

    Literature review

    Diffusion models are the most widely used family for industrial defect synthesis. They learn to remove noise step by step, so generation can be steered by text, structural maps or a reference image.

    Approach How it works Reported result
    SD + ControlNet [1] Edge and depth maps from real PCBs guide generation, so defects follow the circuit layout Detector accuracy 87.5% → 93.4%
    UniPCB [2] Fuses edge, depth and text cues at four resolution levels to keep PCB defects structurally plausible 98.0% mAP@0.5
    DDPM for wafers [3] Generated wafer defects, screened by FID YOLOv8 classification accuracy 98.7%

    Table 1. Diffusion-based defect synthesis in the literature.

    LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) is a fine-tuning technique, not a generative architecture. It keeps the base model frozen and trains only small low-rank matrices added to its layers [Hu et al., 2022]. We don't teach the model to draw from scratch; we nudge its existing visual knowledge toward one specific solder defect. This is why a LoRA can be trained from as few as ~10 real images per class.

    GAN-based

    StyleGAN3 for wafers [6], DT-GAN for defect transfer [7], wafer-dicing augmentation [8]. Trained from scratch, so they need more data.

    Transformers

    DALL·E builds images token by token [4]; Qwen-Image is a 20B diffusion transformer [5]. Strong prompt-following, but too heavy for local VRAM.

    Our choice

    Latent diffusion + LoRA: adapts from ~10 images per class, runs on one local GPU, and builds on the UROP baseline.

    We compared these families against our constraints: very few real images per defect class, and a toolkit that must run locally on a single GPU.

    Model selection

    Approach Outcome Verdict
    VAE variants (β-VAE, perceptual + TV loss) Controllable but low-resolution and blurry Rejected
    Qwen-Image / Qwen-Image-Edit Good quality, but ~100 GB VRAM to train Not viable locally
    Stable Diffusion 1.5 + LoRA Artifacts, outputs unrelated to defects Rejected
    Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium + LoRA Blurry, indistinct defects Rejected
    SDXL Base 1.0 + LoRA Highest fidelity; only model to improve downstream accuracy Adopted

    Table 2. Generative models evaluated in prior work.

    SDXL then went through two optimisation rounds. Natural-language prompts generated by a local Llama 7B model lowered FID but had mixed effects on accuracy. Training one LoRA per defect class ("individual") beat a single shared model on fidelity, FID and accuracy for clear-cut classes; for example, NG-No Solder accuracy rose from 73% to 93%. Individual training was adopted. The team wrapped the pipeline in the AITK web app: setup → training → generation → output.

    Gaps this project addresses

    Gap in prior workflow This project

    SDXL needs >12 GB VRAM, and text-to-image generation can get defect geometry wrong Lighter photorealistic model and image-to-image generation (Section 06)
    No automated batch or per-image quality scoring YOLO-based per-image checks and pass rate (Section 08)

    04

    Defect Taxonomy

    Defects are grouped by their physical failure mechanism, not just their visual appearance. Grounding generation in how a defect actually forms helps keep synthetic images physically plausible. Mechanisms are drawn from electronics-soldering literature [9–12] and will be confirmed against TE's process.

    OK: accepted weld

    Appearance: both pins present, even solder fillet, correct alignment.
    Mechanism: good wetting. Molten solder reacts with the electrode metal to form a thin, continuous intermetallic (IMC) layer, which gives an even fillet and a sound bond [9, 10].
    Real samples available: 200

    NG-Single

    Appearance: only one pin present in the joint.
    Mechanism: one electrode is not present at joining, likely a part-feeding or handling failure upstream. No specific literature found yet; to confirm with TE.
    Real samples available: 30

    NG-No Solder

    Appearance: bare pins, no solder deposit.
    Mechanism: non-wetting: solder does not bond to oxidised or contaminated surfaces, or when the flux is not active enough or the joint is not heated enough [11]. It can also occur if no solder is supplied.
    Real samples available: 25

    NG-Misaligned

    Appearance: pins offset or not parallel.
    Mechanism: a positional offset before joining. Placement studies show part position and solder position and volume drive shift; surface tension of molten solder can pull parts back into line (self-alignment), but small parts and large offsets are not fully corrected [12].
    Real samples available: 24

    05

    Application Architecture

    The application architecture was redesigned to separate the user interface, API services, background GPU execution, model training, image generation and workspace storage. The objective is to support different manufacturing datasets through a configurable and maintainable platform rather than a machine-specific application.

    In addition to optimising the diffusion model, the FYP redesigns the earlier application architecture to support a more flexible, scalable and maintainable synthetic-image generation workflow. The objective is to support multiple manufacturing datasets and defect classes without requiring users to install or configure machine-learning software individually.

    Previous Architecture

    Technical basis: The previous application architecture and its limitations are documented in the project predecessor's UROP report [22].

    The previous implementation integrated Electron/React, Python Flask, SDXL LoRA training and Diffusers inference into a locally deployed desktop application. Datasets, model checkpoints and generated images were stored on the user's machine.

    Electron / React Desktop interface
    →
    Flask Python backend
    →
    Local GPU LoRA + Diffusers
    →
    Local Storage
    Local GPU dependency

    Training and generation depended on the GPU available on the user's computer.

    Environment complexity

    Installation required compatible Python, Node.js, CUDA, PyTorch and machine-learning dependencies.

    Machine-bound access

    Each workstation required individual installation, configuration and troubleshooting.

    Limited centralised orchestration

    Coordinating multiple GPU jobs and sharing computational resources was difficult.

    Current Architecture

    Technical basis: The redesigned architecture uses established asynchronous task-processing and API frameworks [23–25].

    The redesigned backend separates request handling, dataset management, training orchestration, inference execution and artifact storage. FastAPI provides REST endpoints while Redis and Celery coordinate computationally expensive background jobs.

    Future deployment Docker-based platform Centralised services and GPU resource management

    Workspace Isolation and Training Batch Management

    Technical basis: Workspace isolation and training-batch management are implementation decisions of the current FYP, rather than features established by a cited research paper.

    Each workspace maintains its own dataset classes, training configurations, model checkpoints and generated images. This separation allows the application to support different manufacturing applications without mixing their training artifacts.

    Training batches group related class-specific runs under one batch identifier. Each run retains its configuration and checkpoints, while generation requests can select the completed batch and resolve the corresponding class-specific LoRA automatically.

    Design consideration The current implementation uses workspace-isolated filesystem storage. PostgreSQL-backed metadata management and more comprehensive containerised deployment remain future scaling directions.

    Configurable Training and Generation APIs

    Technical basis: The API design builds on FastAPI's validated request models and the configurable training and inference interfaces provided by the underlying machine-learning frameworks [23, 26].

    Earlier workflows were comparatively predefined. Changing model selection or introducing a different generation strategy could require application-code modifications.

    The redesigned API supports configurable JSON requests for selecting base models, LoRA settings, training strategies, checkpoints, inference parameters and generation methods.

    Dynamic base-model selection

    Compatible Stable Diffusion models can be selected through configuration rather than hardcoded into the application.

    Universal training configuration

    Shared training defaults can be applied across multiple classes, with optional class-specific hyperparameter overrides.

    Generation from training runs

    Completed training runs and batches can be selected directly, including intermediate checkpoints and class-specific overrides.

    These interfaces also establish a foundation for the Recommendation Agent, which can eventually propose configurations through the same validated API without modifying the training implementation.

    Deployment status FastAPI, Redis and Celery have been exercised in the local development environment. The fully containerised web deployment is a planned architectural direction rather than a completed production deployment.
    06

    Generation Pipeline

    Pipeline Overview

    Technical basis: The generation pipeline is based on latent diffusion and parameter-efficient adaptation [14, 27].

    We have moved the pipeline from the UROP team's SDXL + LoRA to Realistic Vision 5.1, an SD1.5-based model tuned for photorealistic images. LoRA training now runs on Kohya_ss instead of Hugging Face PEFT, and generation uses Hugging Face Diffusers in text-to-image or image-to-image mode, with image-to-image the more reliable of the two so far (Section 06).

    Before (UROP) Now
    Base model Stable Diffusion XL Base 1.0 Realistic Vision 5.1 (SD1.5) + sd-vae-ft-mse VAE
    Image size 1024 × 1024 512 × 512
    VRAM >12 GB ~6 GB
    LoRA training Hugging Face PEFT + Accelerate Kohya_ss / sd-scripts
    LoRA setup One LoRA per class Shared multiclass or independent class-specific LoRAs
    Generation Text-to-image Txt2Img, Img2Img or Txt2Img + Canny ControlNet

    Table 4. Model and pipeline changes.

    Why we switchedWhen we re-ran the UROP SDXL model, the images were blurry and often did not match their class. SDXL also needs more than 12 GB of VRAM. Realistic Vision gives a stronger photographic prior at about half the memory, which allows faster training and more experiments. The same LoRA works for both text-to-image and image-to-image. We are also checking that the training datasets are clean, since label noise may have contributed to the poor UROP results.

    Captions follow a configurable pattern combining a trigger word, manufacturing-domain description and class-specific defect description. The pipeline supports both a shared multiclass LoRA and independent class-specific LoRAs. In per-class generation, the selected training batch resolves the corresponding adapter and checkpoint automatically.

    Prompts & Captions

    Every caption and prompt follows the same pattern: trigger word + domain + class description. The trigger sldrjnt is kept first (keep_tokens = 1) so the LoRA ties it to this product. The domain is "close-up macro photo of a vertical metal electrode solder joint, dark blurry background".

    Class Description used in captions and prompts
    OK aligned vertically stacked electrodes, top and bottom electrode on the same vertical center axis, centered solder joint
    NG-Misalign misaligned vertically stacked electrodes, top and bottom electrode on different vertical center axes, visible lateral offset at solder joint
    NG-Single vertically stacked electrodes but only one electrode present, missing opposing electrode at the solder joint
    NG-No solder vertically stacked electrodes with no solder, missing solder material between top and bottom electrode

    Table 6. Class descriptions.

    Negative prompt

    horizontal alignment, side-by-side composition, two parallel lines, left and right objects, separate objects, duplicate, deformed, blurry background blobs, text, watermark

    Prompt variations

    Added to vary output: metallic texture and solder shape; lighting direction and exposure; solder appearance and highlights; camera position, magnification and depth of field; oxidation and discolouration.

    07

    Model Optimisation

    Model optimisation investigates how diffusion-model selection, LoRA training strategy and generation conditioning affect the realism and correctness of synthetic manufacturing defect images.

    Experiments were conducted using the available solder-joint inspection dataset, while the application architecture was designed to support other manufacturing datasets and defect types.

    Experimental Approach and Model Selection

    Technical basis: SDXL and LoRA are described in [13, 14]. Realistic Vision V5.1 is documented in [19], while latent diffusion provides the underlying generative framework [27].

    The previous UROP implementation adopted SDXL with LoRA after comparing several generative approaches. This FYP explored SD 1.5-based Realistic Vision V5.1 as a lower-resource alternative for iterative experimentation.

    Realistic Vision was selected for its general photographic prior and compatibility with the existing SD 1.5 LoRA and ControlNet ecosystem. However, a general photorealistic model does not necessarily understand specialised manufacturing geometry.

    Model Role Observation / consideration
    SDXL Base 1.0 Previous UROP baseline Higher computational requirements; strong prior-work results
    Stable Diffusion 1.5 Lower-resource model family More accessible GPU requirements, but specialised geometry remains challenging
    Realistic Vision V5.1 Current experimental base model Reasonable photographic appearance, but electrode and solder artifacts persist

    Shared Multiclass versus Class-Specific LoRA

    Technical basis: LoRA uses low-rank trainable updates to adapt pretrained models [14]. The shared-versus-per-class comparison presented here is based on the project's own experiments and earlier UROP findings [22].

    Two LoRA training strategies were investigated. The first trains one adapter on all defect classes. The second trains a separate adapter for each class.

    Experiment A — Shared Multiclass LoRA

    A single adapter learns from all classes. This provides more examples of common manufacturing structure and simplifies checkpoint management.

    Observed issue: Class-concept interference can occur, with NG-Misalign generations sometimes exhibiting OK-like geometry.

    Experiment B — Per-Class LoRA

    Separate adapters specialise in individual defect classes, reducing direct interference between competing defect concepts.

    Observed issue: Classes containing only 10–15 images remain vulnerable to overfitting, blurred textures and unrealistic component geometry.

    Criterion Shared LoRA Per-Class LoRA
    Training images All selected classes Images from one class
    Adapter count One One per class
    Common domain learning Uses all class examples Limited by class size
    Class interference Potentially greater Potentially reduced
    Main limitation Concept bleeding Few-shot overfitting

    Shared Multiclass LoRA — Generated Examples

    Benefit: One adapter learns shared manufacturing characteristics across multiple classes. Limitation: Class-concept interference can cause an intended misaligned generation to exhibit OK-like electrode alignment.

    Per-Class LoRA — Generated Examples

    Benefit: Each adapter specialises in one defect class, reducing direct competition between class concepts. Limitation: Small datasets can still produce blur, distorted solder and unrealistic component geometry.

    LoRA Hyperparameter Investigation

    Technical basis: The role of low-rank adaptation is established in [14]. The effects of rank, training duration and convolutional adaptation on this solder dataset remain experimental questions rather than conclusions of that paper.

    Training experiments explored adapter capacity, learning rates, training duration, convolutional adaptation and checkpoint selection.

    LoRA Rank and Alpha

    Higher rank increases adapter capacity but also increases training cost and may overfit small datasets.

    Convolutional Adaptation

    Convolutional LoRA was investigated for learning local image characteristics such as metallic texture and component boundaries.

    Training Duration

    Intermediate checkpoints permit comparisons across epochs instead of assuming that the final checkpoint provides the best result.

    The configurable training API also supports optimiser selection, learning-rate scheduling, mixed precision, gradient accumulation, dataset repeats and checkpoint intervals.

    Key consideration Increasing LoRA rank or training duration does not necessarily improve realism. With only a small number of defect examples, higher model capacity may reinforce memorised patterns or generation artifacts.

    Generation Strategy Experiments

    Technical basis: Diffusion-based generation is grounded in denoising probabilistic models and latent diffusion [27, 28]. Image-to-image inference is implemented through Diffusers [26].

    Three generation approaches were investigated to understand the trade-off between structural fidelity, realism and diversity.

    Txt2Img

    Generates from random noise and text prompts. Provides high variation but may produce incorrect component geometry or defects.

    Img2Img

    Begins from a real reference image. Better preserves framing and appearance, but low denoising strength can limit novelty.

    Txt2Img + Canny ControlNet

    Uses reference-image edges to guide generation. Improves structural consistency but depends on edge-map quality.

    Method Strength Limitation
    Txt2Img Generation diversity Unreliable component geometry
    Img2Img Reference fidelity Reduced structural novelty
    Canny ControlNet Spatial guidance Misleading reflection edges and fixed geometry

    Txt2Img and Img2Img Comparison

    Txt2Img provides greater generation freedom but can invent incorrect manufacturing geometry. Img2Img better preserves reference appearance, although low denoising strength may limit diversity.

    Canny ControlNet Experiments

    Technical basis: Canny edge detection was introduced in [29], while ControlNet provides spatial conditioning for pretrained diffusion models [30].

    Canny conditioning was introduced to improve the electrode geometry produced by Txt2Img. Reference images were converted into edge maps, which were supplied to ControlNet during diffusion.

    Reference Image
    →
    Canny Edge Map
    →
    ControlNet + LoRA
    →
    Generated Image

    Canny preprocessing was examined using threshold pairs of 50/100, 100/200 and 150/250. Lower thresholds captured more image features but also detected metallic reflections. Higher thresholds removed some noise while potentially discarding useful component boundaries.

    Observed limitation Canny improved the recognisability of electrode arrangements in some generations, but solder regions remained blurred or physically implausible. Intensity edges did not always correspond to actual solder boundaries.

    Fixed reference geometry also limits controllable defect severity. A prompt requesting greater misalignment can conflict with an edge map containing only a small displacement.

    Canny ControlNet Examples

    Canny ControlNet improves spatial guidance but depends on the quality of the reference edges. Strong reflections, overexposure and soft solder boundaries can create misleading conditioning maps.

    Preliminary Experimental Results

    Technical basis: These results are from the current FYP's preliminary experiments. They should not be interpreted as independently established results from the literature.

    Manual generation experiments were evaluated using intended-class agreement under the current YOLO-based evaluator.

    40%
    Txt2Img — 80/200 intended-class matches
    88%
    Img2Img — 176/200 intended-class matches
    Txt2Img
    40%
    Img2Img
    88%

    Preliminary results: The comparison was reported in the project presentation, slide 26. The percentages represent intended-class agreement under the current YOLO evaluator, not direct measurements of photorealism or downstream classification improvement.

    The preliminary results favour Img2Img under the tested conditions. However, classifier agreement alone does not establish whether synthetic images are realistic, diverse or suitable for training inspection systems.

    Key Findings and Future Improvements

    Technical basis: Potential extensions to structural conditioning are motivated by ControlNet [30]. The proposed dataset-adaptive strategy selection remains future work.

    Finding Proposed Next Step
    Shared LoRA can mix defect concepts Compare shared, per-class and sequential adaptation
    Few-shot training can overfit Evaluate intermediate checkpoints and learning rates
    Txt2Img can invent incorrect geometry Investigate reference and structural conditioning
    Img2Img can limit novelty Study denoising strength and localized editing
    Canny maps may contain reflection artifacts Compare preprocessing and alternative conditioning methods
    Defect severity is difficult to control Investigate prompt-guided, dataset-adaptive editing

    Future work will investigate more flexible generation methods that can adapt to different manufacturing components and defect mechanisms. The objective is not to hardcode solder-joint geometry, but to support dataset-dependent generation strategies through a common API.

    The long-term direction is to connect the generation pipeline with the Recommendation and Evaluation Agents so measured outcomes can guide subsequent configuration choices.

    08

    Tuning Agent

    The tuning agent is Part 2 of our application. Good generation settings differ by dataset and defect class, and are hard to choose without generative-AI experience. The tuning agent evaluates the generated images first and only re-tunes the settings when the images are not good enough, repeating until they pass.

    Agents

    1 · Evaluator

    Verifies that each generated image actually shows the defect it was meant to show, and reports how many pass.

    More details
    • A YOLO26n classifier trained only on real TE images.
    • An image passes if its predicted class matches its intended class.
    • The batch pass rate sets the verdict: Accept, Borderline or Reject.
    See Section 7.2 →
    2 · Decision

    Turns the pass rate into an action: stop and save, or re-tune.

    More details
    • Accept (≥ 80%): keep the passing images, save the settings and end the loop. No tuning needed.
    • Borderline (50–80%): ask the Recommender to search near this run.
    • Reject (< 50%): ask the Recommender to explore different settings.
    • Also stops the loop when the run budget is spent.
    3 · Recommender

    Proposes new training settings, only when the images are not accepted.

    More details

    Inputs: A predefined hyperparameter search space and optimisation history. Future integration will incorporate evaluation scores and feedback from the Decision Agent.

    Method: Optuna's Tree-structured Parzen Estimator (TPE) proposes candidate configurations, which are checked using Pydantic validation.

    Outputs: Validated recommendations for learning rate, LoRA rank and training epochs, with trial history recorded in an Optuna SQLite database.

    See Section 7.6 →

    The loop starts by generating images with the current settings (the defaults on the first run). The Evaluator scores them, the Decision agent gives a verdict, and settings are only re-tuned if the verdict is not Accept.

    Evaluator: YOLO judge

    The Evaluator checks whether each generated image shows its intended defect. A second question, whether the images actually help the inspection model, will be answered by a downstream test planned for Semester 2.

    Ultralytics YOLO is widely used to detect and classify defective products in industry, with high reported accuracy on product images [Qi et al., 2024], including solder defects in automatic optical inspection [Dai et al., 2020].

    # Step What Note
    1 Split dataset Labelled TE solder images split into training, testing and validation sets; 4 classes: OK, NG-Single electrode, NG-No solder, NG-Misalign Real images only
    2 Train YOLO26n classifier trained on 75 real TE images Never trained on synthetic images
    3 Score Pass if predicted class = intended class Pass rule applied to every generated image
    4 Check Recall of at least 90% for every class on held-out real images Needed before the judge is trusted

    Table 8. Setting up and using the YOLO judge.

    Judge results on real images

    Class Recall Correct Notes
    OK 100% 4 / 4 Confidence 1.0
    NG-Single electrode 100% 4 / 4 Confidence 1.0
    NG-No solder 100% 3 / 3 Confidence 1.0
    NG-Misalign 67% 2 / 3 One image read as NG-No solder (confidence 0.81)

    Figure . YOLO judge recall per class on the validation set. Each square is one real validation image; hover or tap a square for its prediction. The dashed line marks the 90% recall target. Switch to Table for the numbers.

    • Clear cues (a missing electrode, no solder) are separated perfectly. Misalignment is a small sideways offset and the smallest class, so it is the weak point.
    • Judge check (≥ 90% recall per class): 3 of 4 classes pass; NG-Misalign does not yet.
    • Validation loss is lowest (≈ 0.10) around epoch 12, then rises to 0.3–0.5 while training loss stays low, so the judge starts to overfit. The best checkpoint is kept (early stopping). Accuracy peaks at 100% (epochs 11–13) and ends at 92.9%.
    Small validation setWith only 3–4 validation images per class, one error moves recall by 25–33%. Next: score the 20-image test split and add more misalignment images.

    Pass rate & Decision agent

    For now the Evaluator uses one metric, scored once per run and per class:

    Pass rate
    share of generated images where predicted class = intended class
    Images that fail are discarded or set aside for checking.

    The pass rate is then passed to the Decision agent, which decides whether the images are good enough or whether the settings need re-tuning. For now, the Decision agent is hard-coded with these pass-rate rules:

    Accept

    Pass rate ≥ 80%. Keep the passing images and save the settings.

    Borderline

    Pass rate 50–80%. The Recommender makes small changes to the settings.

    Reject

    Pass rate < 50%. The Recommender explores new settings.

    Why 80%?The acceptance threshold is set lower for now because data is still limited and we want the loop to keep running. Once there is enough data and testing, the threshold will be raised.
    Known limitationThe YOLO judge does not catch copies of training images or near-identical batches. A near-duplicate check can be added later if needed.

    Results: img2img vs txt2img

    Same YOLO judge, 50 generated images per class (200 per mode). Img2img keeps the real image's structure and passes 88% (176 of 200) → Accept. Txt2img has to invent the geometry and passes only 40% (80 of 200) → Reject, matching our visual inspection.

    Figure . YOLO pass rate per class. Each bar is labelled with its verdict: Accept ≥ 80%, Borderline 50–80%, Reject < 50%. Dashed lines mark the 50% and 80% thresholds.

    • Txt2img rarely produces a missing electrode: NG-Single electrode passes only 12%.
    • Img2img's weakest class is OK (70%): 15 of 50 "OK" images were read as defects.
    • Decision agent applied to these first runs: img2img → Accept; txt2img → Reject (explore new settings).
    CaveatA high pass rate does not prove the images are useful: img2img may stay too close to its reference images. Next: a near-duplicate check and a downstream test.

    Recommender agent

    The Recommender Agent is responsible for proposing new LoRA training configurations when generated images fail to meet the required quality threshold. Within the proposed tuning workflow, the Decision Agent triggers the Recommender when evaluation results are classified as Borderline or Reject. The Recommender uses Optuna's Tree-structured Parzen Estimator (TPE) to search for promising hyperparameter combinations, reducing the need for manual trial-and-error.

    The proposed agent-based optimisation workflow draws on multi-agent hyperparameter optimisation frameworks described by Madiraju and Madiraju [24] and Chaithanya Vijaya [25]. These provide conceptual references for coordinating parameter recommendations, evaluation feedback and subsequent optimisation decisions.

    Inputs

    The current prototype uses a predefined hyperparameter search space and Optuna's recorded trial history. An evaluation adapter converts per-class evaluation results into a numerical score suitable for optimisation. Future integration will incorporate feedback from the Decision Agent to guide subsequent recommendations.

    Method

    Optuna's Tree-structured Parzen Estimator (TPE) proposes candidate configurations based on previous trial results. The first three trials are startup trials, after which TPE uses the accumulated optimisation history. Pydantic validates each configuration against the predefined parameter constraints.

    Outputs

    The Recommender outputs validated configurations containing learning rate, LoRA rank and maximum training epochs. Trial configurations are saved as JSON files, while Optuna records the recommended parameters and associated evaluation scores in a persistent SQLite database.

    Parameter Search Range Purpose
    learning_rate 1 × 10−6 to 5 × 10−4 Controls training update size and stability.
    network_dim 4, 8, 16, 32 Determines LoRA capacity and computational cost.
    max_train_epochs 10–50 Controls training duration and overfitting risk.

    Table 9. Hyperparameter search space implemented in the Optuna-based Recommender Agent.

    Results / progress

    The initial Recommender Agent has been developed using Optuna for hyperparameter optimisation and Pydantic for configuration validation. Preliminary testing focuses on demonstrating the feasibility of the optimisation workflow and its compatibility with the Evaluation Agent before implementing GPU-based training.

    Preliminary Testing
    1 · Simulated Optimisation

    A mock evaluation function was implemented to test the optimisation loop without GPU training. Optuna proposes hyperparameter configurations, validates them using Pydantic, receives simulated scores and records the results for subsequent trials.

    2 · Historical Evaluation

    Existing text-to-image and image-to-image evaluation results are processed to calculate class-level pass rates. These scores are returned to Optuna to verify compatibility between the Recommender and Evaluation Agent.

    3 · YOLO Integration

    An integration script has been developed to connect the Recommender with the YOLO Evaluation Agent. It loads previously generated images, obtains classification results and converts them into an optimisation score. The integration is currently a work in progress, with further testing required to verify successful execution.

    Test 1 · Simulated Optimisation

    To verify the optimisation mechanism without GPU training, a simulated objective function was developed. The function assigns higher scores to hyperparameter configurations closer to predefined target values.

    Mock Evaluation Score
    \[ \begin{aligned} S_{\mathrm{mock}} = 100 &- 20\left| \log_{10}\left(\frac{\eta}{5\times10^{-5}}\right) \right|\\[6pt] &- 10\frac{|r-16|}{16} - 10\frac{|E-30|}{30} \end{aligned} \]

    Here, η represents the learning rate, r represents the LoRA rank, and E represents the maximum number of training epochs.

    The predefined target configuration is a learning rate of 5 × 10−5, LoRA rank of 16 and 30 training epochs.

    These target values were selected solely to construct a simulated objective function. They do not represent experimentally determined optimal training settings.

    This test verifies whether Optuna can propose configurations, receive parameter-dependent feedback and use recorded scores to guide subsequent recommendations.

    Test 2 · Historical Evaluation Feedback

    The second test examines whether existing evaluation results can be converted into a numerical objective suitable for Optuna.

    Historical text-to-image and image-to-image evaluation CSV files are processed to calculate the pass rate for each defect class. The Evaluator Adapter then combines these class-level scores using a macro-average pass rate.

    Macro-average Pass Rate
    \[ S_{\mathrm{evaluation}} = \frac{1}{K} \sum_{k=1}^{K} p_k \]

    Here, K represents the number of evaluated defect classes and pk represents the pass rate of defect class k.

    Each defect class contributes equally to the optimisation score, regardless of the number of images in that class.

    For example, if three defect classes achieve pass rates of 80%, 90% and 70%, the macro-average score is:

    \[ S_{\mathrm{evaluation}} = \frac{0.8+0.9+0.7}{3} = 0.8 \]

    Optuna receives a score of 0.8, corresponding to an 80% macro-average pass rate.

    This test verifies the evaluation-feedback interface. However, the historical scores are obtained from existing datasets rather than images generated using each trial's recommended hyperparameters. Hence, it does not yet demonstrate training-based optimisation.

    Additional Test · YOLO Evaluator Integration

    A separate integration script has been developed to connect the Recommender directly to the YOLO Evaluation Agent. The script loads previously generated images, classifies them using the existing YOLO model and converts the evaluation summary into a numerical score using the same macro-average pass-rate formula as Test 2.

    The integration between the Recommender and YOLO Evaluation Agent is currently a work in progress. While the integration code has been developed, further testing is required. The current implementation evaluates a fixed image dataset, with trial-specific image generation planned for Semester 2.

    Current Limitations and Next Steps

    The preliminary tests demonstrate the feasibility of the Recommender Agent's hyperparameter optimisation mechanism, configuration validation and evaluation-feedback interface. Simulated optimisation verifies that Optuna can use parameter-dependent scores to guide subsequent recommendations, while historical evaluation testing demonstrates compatibility with the Evaluation Agent's scoring format.

    However, the current implementation does not yet perform full closed-loop optimisation, as the recommended hyperparameters are not directly linked to new training and image generation runs.

    In Semester 2, the primary objective is to implement the complete automated feedback-driven hyperparameter optimisation loop by integrating the Recommender Agent with the LoRA training pipeline, image generation, Evaluation Agent and Decision Agent.

    The process will begin with an initial LoRA training run using the default hyperparameter configuration, followed by synthetic defect image generation and evaluation. If the generated images do not meet the required quality threshold, the Decision Agent will trigger the Recommender to propose alternative hyperparameters.

    Each recommended configuration will then be validated and used to retrain the LoRA model and generate a new set of synthetic defect images. The Evaluation Agent will assess these images, and the resulting scores will be returned to Optuna to guide subsequent recommendations.

    This iterative process will continue until the required quality threshold is achieved or the predefined computational budget is exhausted.

    Once the complete loop is operational, its effectiveness will be evaluated by comparing the optimised configurations against manually selected settings and alternative search strategies. The objective is to improve synthetic defect image quality while reducing unnecessary training runs and manual intervention.

    Future Work

    Planned work for Semester 2 (January to May 2027). See the Project Timeline (Section 10) for when each item happens.

    1 · UI/UX application

    Build the application that users work in: a guided, step-by-step flow from uploading images to approving generated results, usable without generative-AI expertise.

    2 · Complete the optimised generation model

    Finalise the generation model and its settings, building on the img2img results from Semester 1.

    3 · Evaluate uploaded datasets

    Extend the Evaluator agent to check the datasets users upload. A classifier will label unlabelled images so they can be used for training. For now, we use labelled datasets.

    4 · Class-based parameter tuning

    Tune parameters per class, so classes that fail or score lower get settings of their own. For example, OK scored 70% with img2img while the other classes scored 90% or more.

    5 · Recommender agent

    Extend the existing Optuna-based Recommender prototype into a complete feedback-driven optimisation system. Integrate it with LoRA training, image generation, the Evaluation Agent and the Decision Agent. Future development will incorporate class-specific evaluation feedback, computational budget constraints and comparisons with alternative optimisation methods.

    6 · Agentic chatbot in the app EXPLORATORY

    Explore an in-app assistant that guides users through the workflow and explains the agents' decisions.
